standard.title: First Nations drama and culture
standard.description: explore the ways that First Nations Australians use drama to continue and revitalise cultures
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore how First Nations Australians use drama to communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place (Y3-4). They understand that drama carries cultural knowledge and is used in community and ceremonial contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore the ways that First Nations Australians use drama to continue and revitalise cultures.

nodes.label: Drama as cultural continuity and revitalisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the difference between drama that maintains existing culture and drama that revitalises culture — and identify examples of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Student distinguishes between cultural maintenance and cultural revitalisation in at least one First Nations drama example.
nodes.typical_width: Students explore how performances that tell stories maintain culture (e.g. narrative drama communicating knowledge about land, sea, sky or waterways); they identify examples showing how cultural expressions change over time using available resources published by First Nations communities and organisations.
wider: Students investigate how a diverse range of First Nations drama makers embed themselves and their communities in drama as a declaration of identity, storytelling and resilience
Students explore how First Nations drama has adapted contemporary forms while maintaining cultural authority and knowledge
nodes.hinge_reason: The concept of revitalisation — that culture can be actively renewed and reclaimed, not just preserved — is what distinguishes this descriptor's inquiry from prior bands; without it, students treat First Nations drama as static heritage rather than living practice.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly distinguish maintenance from revitalisation before examining examples; use culturally authoritative resources and, where possible, First Nations voices explaining their own intentions.

success_criteria: Student explains the difference between cultural maintenance and revitalisation in drama
Student provides a First Nations drama example that illustrates one or both

nodes.label: How drama makers embed identity and community
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify specific ways First Nations drama makers embed identity, community, storytelling and resilience in their work.
nodes.minimum_width: Student describes at least two specific ways a First Nations drama maker uses drama to represent identity or community.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate how drama is used to share cultural narratives; they explore First Nations drama makers' roles in using drama across representative forms; they identify how storytelling, land connection and resilience appear as recurring themes; they use resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians.
wider: Students investigate First Nations drama that explicitly responds to or challenges colonial history — exploring how dramatic form carries political and cultural assertion
Students compare First Nations drama from different communities, identifying both shared themes (land, identity, story) and distinctive cultural expressions

response_modes.reason: First Nations drama is diverse across Country and community; use multiple examples from different makers and communities to ensure students do not reduce it to a single representative narrative.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The diversity of First Nations drama makers, communities, forms and purposes is very broad; engaging with multiple examples develops genuine appreciation of the richness of First Nations dramatic traditions and avoids homogenisation.
success_criteria: Student describes at least two specific ways a First Nations drama maker uses drama to represent identity or community
Student can explain how one of those ways connects to cultural continuity or revitalisation
